title: Do Not Tread Lightly
gist: A widow argues that law, regulation and cultural norms leave families only cremation, burial or donation, blocking preservation of the body even though preservation chemicals and techniques are cheap. She reframes the meaning of life around material legacy and funerary rites as a marker of civilization.

insights.claim: After death, a body's custody passes to the morgue, coroner and funeral home, and the funeral director said only two options exist: disposal or donation.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Regulation confines the death-care market to a narrow product set, leaving unserved demand for preservation.
insights.quote: the funeral director ultimately informed me there are only two: disposal or donation

insights.claim: Cremation heats remains to 1,400-1,800 degrees Fahrenheit and pulverizes them, destroying all DNA; ashes are distinguishable only by paperwork chain of custody.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Cremation, the cheap default, is irreversible and forecloses any future biological use.

insights.claim: Shared-coffin burial is essentially impossible because exhumation requires PPE, negative pressure tents, disinfectants, and thousands of dollars in funeral home, cemetery, vault, casket and legal fees, and is legally permitted only for relocation or forensic examination.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Regulatory and fee layers make post-burial access prohibitively costly.

insights.claim: Most cemeteries require each casket in a separate reinforced vault, so burial in the vast majority of cases forfeits any future physical presence with the loved one.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Vault rules lock in the irreversibility of burial.

insights.claim: Body brokers and research institutions are granted far greater control over a donated body, for a few thousand dollars per body, than owners or next of kin can obtain at any price.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Asymmetry between institutional and family rights over bodies is a regulatory-capture signal.

insights.claim: In 2023 Oregon passed legislation allowing patients to keep amputated body parts after patients reportedly refused lifesaving surgeries that would have destroyed or discarded the limbs.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: A precedent that incremental legal expansion of bodily rights is possible.

themes.theme: Cost and regulatory barriers to preservation

insights.claim: Preservation technology has become cheap: the chemicals that preserved Rosalia Lombardo for a century cost barely $100 today, and excarnation of a medium mammal skeleton costs several hundred to several thousand dollars, less than a moderately nice coffin.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Cost is not the binding constraint on human preservation; law is.

insights.claim: Legal barriers, regulatory burden and a tight market of qualified professionals inflate preservation costs even for non-human remains, and applying such skills to human remains is never permitted.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Regulation, not technology, creates scarcity and potential pricing power in preservation services.

insights.claim: Abuse-of-a-corpse laws are cited as justification for the restrictions, yet the author argues the state assumes everyone wants the same anonymous rot or cremation regardless of individual personality.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Uniform rules ignore heterogeneous preferences, an unserved niche for differentiated offerings.

insights.claim: The Sedlec Ossuary contains bones from at least 40,000 skeletons, shaped into columns, a chandelier and a coat of arms, showing the line between honoring and exploiting the dead has always been blurry.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for respectful display undercuts the premise of the restrictions.

insights.claim: Contrary to warnings about a predatory funeral industry upselling grieving customers, the author was repeatedly steered toward the cheap, easy, convenient option such as cardboard caskets and cremation.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Industry incentives and norms push low-cost disposal, shaping demand toward commodity services.

insights.claim: The wealthy are sold disappearance too: the most expensive venue toured was a natural cemetery barring embalming chemicals, with tiny or absent grave markers and overgrown, hard-to-traverse terrain, certified by the Green Burial Council.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Premium death-care is trending toward green, anonymous burial rather than lasting memorials.

insights.claim: Limits on choice over the post-sentient state stem from a confluence of regulatory capture, inflated costs and unquestioned cultural assumptions.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Frames death-care as a captured, culturally entrenched market ripe for disruption.

insights.claim: The author shifted from sentientism to a maximalist view of life's meaning: consciousness lasts mere years while the material effects of works and physical form can endure for centuries.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Values placed on durable material legacy support long-horizon, legacy-oriented products and projects.

insights.claim: Funerary rites embody three necessary qualities of civilization: valuing material legacy, honoring neighbors' wishes when unobserved, and belief in a shared future, which enabled pyramids, churches and scientific knowledge finished after their architects died.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Links long-term institutional capacity to respect for the dead and future-orientation.

insights.claim: Mummification practices are documented on every continent humans have lived on, including hunter-gatherer remains in Asia dating to 10,000 BC, so modern regulation marks a departure from an ancient, widespread desire to preserve the body.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Preservation demand is historically universal, suggesting latent demand.

insights.claim: Cryonics has not yet solved freezing human tissue without water crystallizing and destroying cellular structure, and companies must be subscribed to in advance to retrieve a body at the moment of death.
insights.speaker: R. B.
insights.so_what: Cryonics remains technically unproven, leaving preservation alternatives as the practical option.
